title: Tensor Conversion and Interoperability
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of tensor conversion and interoperability in a PyTorch workflow.
Apply a small example of tensor conversion and interoperability and interpret the output.
Identify a relevant limitation, debugging check, or reproducibility concern.

content.intro: Tensor Conversion and Interoperability: Tensors are the main data structure in PyTorch. Shape describes the size of each axis, rank is the number of axes, and dtype determines how values are represented. In this lesson, use a small example to make the inputs, outputs, and boundary conditions explicit.
content.why_it_matters: Most early PyTorch errors are easier to diagnose when shape, rank, dtype, and indexing are checked before a tensor enters a model. For this lesson, focus on conversion to and from numpy and the evidence you can collect from a controlled example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Read a tensor as both values and metadata: shape, rank, dtype, device, and indexing behavior determine which operations are valid. The source topics for this lesson are: Conversion to and from NumPy, CPU and accelerator transfers, Contiguous versus non-contiguous tensors. Keep each topic connected to a checkable input/output behavior.

content_blocks.title: Read the example
content_blocks.text: Follow the dimensions as tensors are created, reshaped, indexed, broadcast, reduced, or converted. Keep the example small enough to inspect each intermediate result. content_blocks.title: Guided PyTorch example
content_blocks.code:
import torch
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0])
arr = x.numpy()
print(arr.tolist())
print(torch.from_numpy(arr).shape)

content.task: Try it yourself: Create tensors of ranks 0 through 3, reshape a range tensor, and assert both the final shape and element count. Record the observed result and one limitation; do not report an unrun training or performance result as measured.

troubleshooting.symptom: A tensor operation raises a shape, dtype, or device mismatch.
troubleshooting.check: Print .shape, .dtype, and .device for each input. Resolve the mismatch intentionally instead of changing dimensions blindly.

troubleshooting.symptom: The example fails because an optional package or accelerator is unavailable.
troubleshooting.check: Check the installed PyTorch/package versions and device availability. Use the official installation selector and run the CPU-compatible path where appropriate.

troubleshooting.symptom: The result differs across runs or machines.
troubleshooting.check: Fix the seed where useful, record versions and inputs, and document operations that remain nondeterministic or hardware dependent.

common_mistakes.problem: Relying on assumptions instead of inspecting the data or output.
common_mistakes.why: Many ML failures come from incorrect shapes, labels, preprocessing, or execution mode rather than a syntax error.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect representative inputs and add assertions for the expected shape, dtype, range, or behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing training-time behavior with inference-time behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Dropout, normalization, gradient tracking, and optimizer updates can change how a model behaves.
common_mistakes.fix: Do not reshape a tensor by guessing dimensions; preserve the element count and verify the resulting axis meanings.

common_mistakes.problem: Using a current or experimental API without recording its version assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Hardware support and ecosystem APIs can change independently of the core package.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin compatible dependencies, record the environment, and test after upgrades.
